title: Block close: the middle centuries
hookLine: cathedrals and crusades, mystics and plague, saints and scandals

lines: ANY ONE OF THEM IS TRUE.
PICK ONLY ONE, AND IT LIES.
cards: Lay the whole block out on a table, like photos from a long trip. A cathedral floor with a labyrinth set into the stone. A knight's sword raised over a city.
Francis bending to kiss a leper's hand. A cart of the dead in a plague year. A monk in a forest leaving bread out for a bear.
A pope scolded in a letter by a young woman from Siena. A man burned for his preaching. A press printing Bibles.
Pick up any one photo and it tells you something true. Pick up only one, and it lies.

teach.h: FROM CLUNY TO THE PRINTING PRESS.
teach.b: This block began at Cluny, with monks praying in shifts so the prayer never stopped, and with the slow, sad parting of the churches of east and west.
Then came Anselm's faith seeking understanding, Bernard's plain white abbeys and Hildegard's music; Francis, Clare and Dominic, and Elizabeth of Hungary with bread in her apron.

Aquinas wrote vast books and then called them straw. Dante climbed toward the love that moves the sun. In the east, Gregory Palamas taught stillness and light, and Rublev painted three angels at an open table.
Julian spoke through her window, Catherine wrote to a pope, Joan stood trial, and Margery wept.
And the same centuries hold the crusades, cities sacked in Christ's name, the burning of Jan Hus, and the plague that emptied whole households.
Some tellers keep only the light: the saints and the spires. Others keep only the shadow: the swords and the scandals. Both versions are easier, and both are false.

Jesus has a parable about this, a field where wheat and weeds come up together. The servants want to rip the weeds out, and the owner says, in the King James Bible: "Let both grow together until the harvest."
And Paul says the treasure is real, but the containers are clay: "we have this treasure in earthen vessels." Christians read those lines in more than one way.
But they give a way to hold this block: the beauty doesn't cancel the failure, and the failure doesn't cancel the beauty. Next comes a church that knows it needs reform.

how: Christians remember the saints of the medieval church on their feast days, and churches have also made public confessions and apologies for wrongs done in Christ's name, including the crusades.

games.q: you're telling a friend the story of the medieval church in one minute. what do you leave in?
o: only the saints and the cathedrals.
only the crusades and the scandals.
games.why: the block ends here: the beauty doesn't cancel the failure, and the failure doesn't cancel the beauty. wheat and weeds grow together.

practice: Bring to mind a person, a group or a place you love that has also let you down: a family, a team, a church, a town, maybe yourself.

In one hand hold one thing about it that's beautiful, in the other one thing that went wrong, and don't let either hand drop or rush to make them balance. If you pray, you can offer both hands to God together.

wordCard.voice: Earthen vessels. Paul's image for the church in these middle centuries: a real treasure carried in breakable containers, the beauty alongside the failure.

carryVoice: Your line: both are true. A whole block of centuries, closed. Day eight hundred fifty.
